units.en: ⟦0⟧ Represents the room that the division takes up while fighting at the front line. In order to fit into battle, the division needs to fit into the combat width provided by the battlefield. The less width that each division takes, the more divisions that can fire upon the enemy at the same time. However, making many thin divisions also has its tradeoffs. Different battalion types increase the combat width of a division by a different amount. For example, infantry and armoured battalions use 2 width, artillery battalions use 3 width, and anti-tank and anti-air battalions use 1 width. Support companies do not increase the combat width of a division (see ⟦1⟧ for details). The Mass Assault ⟦2⟧ tree has options that reduce the combat width of ⟦3⟧ battalions, while the mountaineer special forces doctrine tree with ⟦4⟧ has an option that reduces the combat width of ⟦5⟧ battalions. The combat width for a division is the ⟦6⟧ of the combat width of all Battalions. Combat width notes: The normal maximum combat width provided by the battlefield varies by terrain. If attacking divisions come from more than one province, then extra width is added to the battlefield for each province, based on the type of terrain that is being attacked. Certain combat tactics can increase or decrease a battle's combat width. It is best to use divisions whose combat widths are factors of the combat width of the terrain you intend to fight in, as this allows you to use as many battalions as possible without sustaining a combat width penalty. Only full divisions can join a fight. Fielding more divisions than the battlefield combat width supports will result in penalties. When this happens, the Battle Interface will automatically put these extra divisions into reserve. Frontage Reduction can reduce the amount of width taken up by divisions, thus allowing more to be used or slightly bigger divisions to be fielded.

⟦0⟧ Represents what proportion of the division is made up of battalions which are hardened and protected, that is, how "hard" the division is. It is the proportion of hard attacks to soft attacks that an incoming unit receives. Units with more hardness will take less soft attack and more hard attack, while units with less hardness will take more soft attack and less hard attack. Different battalions have different levels of hardness. For example, ⟦1⟧ are very soft (0%), ⟦2⟧ are slightly harder (20%), ⟦3⟧ are fairly hard (60-75%), ⟦4⟧ are quite hard (90%), and ⟦5⟧ are the hardest (100%). Multiply this with the attacker's hard attack and multiply 1 - Hardness (i.e. softness) with the attacker's soft attack to find out how many attacks are made against the division. Divisions with high hardness will suffer more of the hard attacks and fewer of the soft attacks directed at them. The hardness for the division is the ⟦6⟧ of those of all line battalions, but not support companies.

⟦0⟧ capacity: How much ⟦1⟧ a unit can store. Higher fuel capacity means that the unit will be able to operate at full capacity longer when it lacks fuel supply. Most units that consume fuel will add 96⟦2⟧ hours' worth of their fuel usage to the division's fuel capacity, though there are ways to increase this. The stat for the division is the ⟦3⟧ of those of all battalions and companies.

Fuel Usage: How much fuel a unit uses while it is operating. Land units with fuel consumption will consume fuel when moving, in combat, or training. Divisions low on fuel can only be refueled in provinces with enough ⟦0⟧. Using ⟦1⟧ support companies can lower a division's fuel usage. The stat for the division is the ⟦2⟧ of those of all battalions and companies, though some support companies do not increase fuel usage despite requiring equipment that normally requires fuel.
Paradrop: A simple true or false check if the division can be ⟦0⟧. For it to be true, all line battalions must be ⟦1⟧. However, most support companies can be mixed in freely.

Special Forces Cap: The amount of special forces battalions that a country can field is capped based on the total amount of non-special forces battalions it has deployed. Divisions cannot be changed, trained, given a different template or have their template adjusted if that would result in exceeding that cap. See ⟦0⟧.

Each division will require a certain amount of ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, and training time to produce. Most of these values are simply a ⟦2⟧, except training time, which is based on the ⟦3⟧ training time of any Battalion or Company. Reference ⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧.
⟦0⟧ can influence the performance of different unit types in offense, defence and even movement. Terrain modifiers are ⟦1⟧ between all Battalions, but those of Support Companies are ⟦2⟧.

NOTE: The table below is not fully accurate. The table below is prepared using first generation equipment. Detailed information for subsequent generations will be found in ⟦0⟧ and for a comparison of equipment of equivalent generation: ⟦1⟧. Generally non-combat statistics are defined per battalion. But combat statistics are a function of equipment and thus not static. Additionally, battalions add modifiers to its equipment. For example, a Marine combat battalion adds +30% Breakthrough to its infantry equipment while an artillery support company has a -40% Soft Attack, -40% Hard Attack, -40% Defence, and -40% Breakthrough to its artillery equipment. If a battalion uses multiple types of equipment, the stats are a sum of all the equipment used. For example, Mechanized battalions use both Weapon and Mechanized equipment (with a 10% bonus to Weapon Soft Attack and 500% bonus to Weapon Hard Attack). Support Equipment adds nothing to combat stats.
Most land unit battalions can be placed in brigade columns and are often referred to as ⟦0⟧. Battalions that need to be placed in the support column are instead called ⟦1⟧. See ⟦2⟧ for more details.
